translations.text: Discourse of our blessed father Basil on the saying of Moses the prophet, in which he says: "Take heed to yourself."
The power of using speech was given to us by our Creator, God,

so that we might reveal the thoughts of the heart to one another, and, for the sake of sharing what is in our minds, each of us might bring forth from the treasuries of the heart and reveal to his neighbor counsel about what is better.
For if our souls were visible and manifest in their nakedness, all the thoughts of our hearts would be plain to one another.
Since, then, our soul is hidden within this covering of flesh, words and reasonings are therefore needed to reveal the thoughts hidden in the depths of the soul.
But when the thought of our heart finds the voice of speech, immediately, as if in a boat,
it passes through the intervening air and reaches from the speaker to the hearer; and if it finds calm and good quiet there,
immediately, as if into waveless harbors, it enters fully into the ears of the hearers.
But if some tumult from the hearers rises against it like a fierce wave, then it is dissipated in the air and sinks.
So give this word calm through your silence; perhaps something useful and profitable may be found in it. For the word of truth
is hard to grasp, and if someone does not hold on to it well, it quickly escapes and flees. For the Holy Spirit has so arranged it,
that it should be narrow and small, that in few words it should signify great power, and again that because of its brevity it should be easy to remember.
The natural virtue of speech is this: that its power should not be hidden by its obscurity and lack of clarity, nor again that it should be excessively wordy and run on idly and vainly over matters,
but that it should be fitting and beautiful in both respects, as is the saying that we have now read from the books of Moses the prophet [?],
which you lovers of learning surely remember, unless because of its smallness it has slipped past your ears.
And the saying is this: "Take heed to yourself, lest a hidden word of lawlessness arise in your heart."
For we are easily carried away toward sin of the mind; and therefore he who alone formed our hearts,
knew that most sins are accomplished by the mind, and therefore he commanded us first of all to purify the mind.
For regarding that by which we sin quickly and in an instant, he has commanded us greater zeal and greater caution.
For just as skilled physicians caution beforehand those who are weak in body,
so too the physician of souls saw this weakness of ours and our quickness toward sin of the mind, and therefore he cautions us with strong teaching.
For bodily deeds require time as well, and opportunity, labor, helpers, and other means,
but the movements of the mind occur without need of time and are accomplished without labor; they happen equally at every time.
Therefore it often happens that someone among the haughty and proud has the outward appearance of purity, and often, while sitting among them,

While those around him call him blessed for his virtue, he suddenly goes off in his mind to the place of sin, by that unseen movement of the heart, and sees those deeds in the imagination of his mind.
He pictures some indecent conversation, and in that wholly unseen place of the soul he portrays the deed and accomplishes the sin, unknown to all and without witness,
until there comes the one who brings to light the hidden things of darkness and reveals the counsels of the heart. Take heed, therefore,
that there be no hidden word of lawlessness in your heart, for whoever looks at a woman with lust has committed adultery.
For bodily deeds are hindered by many things, but whoever sins in the mind accomplishes the sin with the very swiftness of his thoughts.
And therefore, where sin is so quickly accomplished, we need diligent watchfulness, for it says:
"Lest there be a hidden word of lawlessness in your heart." But let us also look at the beginning of that saying.
"Take heed to yourself," it says. All creatures have by nature, from God the Creator, the care of themselves, and if you consider it well, you will find that many of the irrational animals,
without being taught, have a hatred of everything harmful, and again, by that natural power, they recognize the things that are beneficial to them and seek them out.
For this reason God has also given us this great commandment, so that what they have by nature, we may have with the help of reason,
and what the irrational animals have unknowingly from nature, we may acquire through watchfulness and the understanding of our thoughts.
And let us be keepers of those gifts given by God; that is, let us flee from sin,
as the irrational animals flee from poisonous and deadly foods, and let us pursue righteousness, as they seek good pasture.
Take heed to yourself, therefore, so that you may be able to distinguish good from evil and the harmful from the beneficial.
Now since there are two kinds of watching, one being the seeing of visible things with the bodily eye, and the second,
that one should see all things with the intellectual eye of the soul and be on guard, now if we were to say
that the prophet spoke this saying about these visible eyes, we would at once find it impossible, for how could anyone see himself entirely with his own eye?
For the eye cannot even see itself, nor reach to the crown of the head, nor examine the back, nor the face, nor the inner organs.
It is wicked, then, to say that the commandments of the Holy Spirit are impossible; rather, this commandment speaks of those spiritual eyes of the mind: "Take heed to yourself,"
that is, be wary on every side and keep that eye of the soul sleepless in guarding yourself,
for you are walking among snares, and hidden traps have been laid by the enemy on every side.
Therefore be wary in every way, so that you may be saved like a gazelle from the snare and like a bird from the trap.
For the gazelle, when it is wary and on its guard, remains uncaught because of the sharpness of its eyes;
for this reason it is called sharp-sighted. And likewise the bird, when it is on its guard, rises above the trap by its wing.
Therefore see to it that you are not perhaps found more foolish and more negligent than even the beasts in guarding yourself.
Do not in any way fall into those snares and be hunted down, captured by the devil to do his will.
"Take heed therefore to yourself" means this: take heed to your own self alone, and not to those external things.
For by "ourselves" is meant the soul and the mind, by which we have been created in the image of God.
But what is "ours" is the body and these bodily senses, while the external things are possessions and the crafts of this world and the other affairs of this life.
Now therefore this saying tells us this: do not merely take care of the body, and do not seek its ease,
health, beauty and the fulfilment of desires; nor again marvel at possessions, glory and power,
nor esteem greatly anything else among the affairs of this passing world, neglecting your true life by seeking after it.
But take heed to yourself, which is your soul, and adorn it and care for it,
so that through vigilance you may wash away every stain that has come upon it from wickedness, cleanse it of all the filth of sins, and adorn it and make it shine with all the beauty of the virtues.
Examine yourself, who you are; understand your own nature, for your body is mortal but your soul immortal, and our life is twofold:
the one is this life of the body, which quickly passes away, and the other is that of the soul, which is boundless and without end.
Take heed therefore to yourself: do not linger among these passing things as though they did not pass away, nor those things that do not pass away, as though they were passing,
disregard. Hold your body of no account [?], for it is mortal and will pass away. Care for the soul, a thing immortal.
Govern yourself with all vigilance, so that you may know how to give each its due portion, so that you may give the body food and clothing,
which it needs by nature, and to the soul the teaching of the fear of God, a strict way of life, the struggle for the virtues, and rising above the passions.

Do not fatten the body, and do not occupy yourself in the tumult of bodily affairs, for since "the flesh lusts against the spirit and the spirit against the flesh, and these are opposed to one another,
see that you do not perhaps aid the flesh and give great strength to what is inferior. For just as in the swing of the scales, if you weigh down the one side,
you undoubtedly lighten the other, so it is with the body and the soul, for the excess of the one produces the deficiency of the other.
For when the body is at ease and weighed down with fatness, then the power of the mind becomes weak and feeble,
but when the soul rejoices and, through training in good works, is raised up to its own glory, then the tyranny of the body withers away.
This same teaching is good for the sick and profitable for the healthy too. For just as physicians instruct the sick to take care of themselves and not to neglect anything
that may be good for their healing, so also the Word, the physician of our souls, wishes by this small medicine to heal the soul that has been made sick by sin.
Take heed therefore to yourself, so that you may receive a healing medicine suited to your sin.
If your sin is great and heavy, you also need a great confession: bitter tears, intense vigil, unceasing fasting.
But if your sin is light and small, let your repentance likewise only be equal to it.
Take heed to yourself, so that you may recognize both the health of the soul and its sickness.
For many, because of their great heedlessness, have great and incurable diseases and do not even know whether they have any disease at all.
But great benefit comes from teaching even to those who are healthy in their deeds, for this same teaching both heals the weak and perfects the healthy.
For each one of us disciples of the word is a servant of some one work among the works that have been commanded to us by the Gospel.
For "in this great house, which is the Church, there are found not only vessels of gold and silver,
but also of wood and of clay," and also crafts of many kinds, for there are "in the temple of God,
which is the Church of the living God," hunters, travelers, master builders, builders, farmers, shepherds, athletes, soldiers.
To all of these this brief saying applies; it teaches each one diligence in his own work and purity of mind:
If you are a hunter sent by the Lord, who said:
"Behold, I send many hunters, and they shall hunt on every mountain," take good heed lest the game escape you,
the game you seek, so that you may capture those who have been made wild by wickedness and lead them to the life-giving word of truth.
If you are a traveler, like the one who says:
"Let my steps be directed," take heed to yourself, so that you do not turn aside from the way and do not swerve to the right or to the left; walk on the royal road.
Again, let the master builder lay without error the foundation of faith, which is Jesus Christ.
Let the builder see how he builds: let him build up not wood, nor hay, nor reed, but gold and silver and precious stones.
If you are a shepherd, again take heed, lest you neglect anything among those in your flock.
And this means that you are to bring back the one who has strayed, bind up the one who is broken, and heal the one who is weak.
If you are a farmer, dig around the unfruitful fig tree and put on it whatever will help it to bear fruit.
If you are a soldier, strive for the Gospel, wage the good warfare against the evil spirits and against the passions of the flesh,
take up all the armor of the Spirit, and do not entangle yourself in the affairs of the world, so that you may please the commander.
If you are an athlete, take heed to yourself, lest you ever transgress the law of the athletes, for no one is crowned unless he competes according to the rules.
Imitate Paul, how he ran and contended and fought. And you too, then, as a good runner, keep the eye of the soul unresting,
shield your vital members with the spreading of your hands, and let your eyes be on your opponent as you move.
Run toward what lies ahead: "So run that you may obtain." In battle, fight against those invisible fighters.
This is what the word of life wants: that you should always live not in negligence or in sleep, but that you should guard yourself carefully and wakefully.
The day would fail me if I tried to recount the kinds of those who help the gospel of Christ and the power of this commandment, how it is suited to all and good.
Guard yourself, be careful and discerning, a keeper of the present and one who foresees the future.
Do not let the present slip away through negligence, and do not imagine things that do not yet exist, or things to come, as if you had them in your hands.
Or do young men not have this sickness by nature? And through lightness of mind, do they not imagine what they are waiting for as if they already had it?
For whenever they are in quiet and solitude, they form unreal fantasies, and through the facility of their minds they wander everywhere and rehearse the splendors of life:
great old age, many children, honor from everyone. And since they cannot stop anywhere, they then rise to still higher things, imagining that they acquire great mansions,
filled with treasure of every kind, and that they acquire as much land as the vanity of their mind pictures, and they store the revenues from these in treasuries of vanity.
To all this they add flocks and herds, countless multitudes of slaves, governorships and leadership of nations, wars.
They devise victories and kingship through the vanity of their mind, and they rehearse all this as if they already had it in their hands.
But this is the sickness of an idle and negligent soul, to see dreams while the body is awake.
And from such [?] looseness of mind and vanity of thoughts this saying guards us, and as with a bridle it restrains that restlessness of mind, and says:
"Guard yourself," and do not rehearse those unreal things, but manage well the things in which you actually are.
And again, the lawgiver spoke this saying for the healing of another passion as well,
for since all of us are more eager to investigate the errors of another than our own, for this reason he says:
Cease investigating the affairs of another; do not give your mind leisure to scrutinize the sins of another, but guard yourself and turn the eye of your soul to seeing your own deeds.
For many, as the Lord says, see the speck in their brother's eye, but do not perceive the beam in their own eyes.
But you, do not cease scrutinizing yourself, whether your life is directed according to the commandments of the Son of God, and do not investigate those outside,
so as to find someone's blemish, like that Pharisee, oppressive and arrogant, who stood and justified himself and despised the tax collector.
But do not cease judging and investigating yourself, lest perhaps you have sinned in thought, or fallen through the tongue, or done something improper by the deed of your hands.
And if you find many sins in yourself, and you will certainly find them, because you are human, then say the words of the tax collector:
"God, be merciful to this sinner." "Take heed to yourself": for this saying, if you are in glory and delight, will then present itself to you as something useful,
like a good counselor, and will remind you of the conditions of human life; and again, if you are distressed in trials, then too may it become a comforter of your heart,
so that you neither come to wicked pride because of your high position, nor again are undone by despair in your afflictions.
If you are adorned with wealth, and boast of the nobility of your parents, and rejoice in your homeland, in the beauty of your body, and in the honor you receive from everyone,
look at yourself: you are mortal, for you are earth and will return to earth.
Look at those who before you took delight in that same kind of glory.
Where are those who held power over cities? Where are those orators who were so hard to contend with?
Where are those splendid horsemen, those commanders and generals and tyrants?
Are they not all dust and fable? Are not the memorials of their lives left in only a few bones?
Look down into the graves, if you can distinguish who is the slave and who is the lord, who is the poor man and who is the rich.
Distinguish, if you can, the prisoner from the king, the strong from the weak, and the beautiful from the ugly.
For if you remember human nature in this way, you will never become puffed up; and you will remember it, if only you take heed to yourself.
Again, if you are fallen and lowly, poor and born of the poor, without a home and without a city, lacking even your daily food, if you tremble before the powerful
and fear everyone because of your poverty, do not give yourself up for lost, and do not cast away all good hope because you have nothing enviable in your circumstances,
but lift up your soul to the good things that have been given to you by God, and also to those that he has promised to give you at the last.
First, you are a human being, alone among all created beings created by the hand of God. Is this alone not enough for the highest joy,
if one rightly and fittingly understands what it is to be created by the very hands of God, the Maker of all?
Then again, understand this also: you were made in the image of God the Creator, and if you wish,
you can attain the honor of the angels by good conduct; and a rational soul has been given to you,
by which you understand God, perceive with your mind the nature of created things, and harvest the precious fruit of wisdom.
All the moving creatures of the earth, domestic and wild, and all that live in the waters and that fly in the air, are slaves and subjects to you.
Was it not you who invented all the arts and built cities and devised everything useful and delightful?
Are not the depths of the seas a path for you because of your reason? Do not earth and sea serve your life?
Or do not the air and the sky and the ranks of the stars show you their own order?
Why then are you faint-hearted because you have no horses harnessed with silver?
— But behold, the sun has been given to you, which by its mighty and swift course makes you shine with light every day.
Do you not have the splendors of silver and gold? — But you have the moon, which beautifully illumines you with its light.
Do you not sit in gold-plated chariots? — But you have feet as your chariot, grown together with you by nature.
Why then do you call blessed those who have acquired that gross and heavy treasure and need other people's feet for walking? Do you not lie on a bed of ivory?
— But you have the earth, more precious than much ivory, and you will sleep on it with good and carefree sleep.
Do you not have a gold-plated ceiling? — But you have the sky, which covers you with the indescribable beauty of the stars.
And all this is human; but what shall we say of the things that are higher? — For your sake God became man.
The grace of the Holy Spirit, the abolition of death, the hope of resurrection, the divine commands that perfect your life,
going to God by means of his commandments, the kingdom of heaven prepared, crowns of righteousness made ready — if you take upon yourself the labors of virtue.
If you understand well, you will find all this and more than this within yourself,
and what you have, you will use well, and over what you lack, you will not become faint-hearted.
And in everything, watching over yourself will be of great benefit to you,
for even if anger and the passion of wrath master you and draw you toward improper and disorderly words and beastly deeds,
if you watch over yourself, you will calm that wrath and make it gentle, like an untamed and fierce colt,
when you touch it with the goad of reason and flog it as with a whip, and restrain your tongue as well, and do not let your hands loose upon the one who has provoked you.
Again, if evil desires excite your soul and draw you toward foul deeds, if you watch over yourself and understand
that the pleasure of that moment is going to reach an end of bitterness, and that the excitement and stirring that now comes upon our flesh from desire
gives birth to that venomous worm which will torment us without dying in Gehenna, and that the burning of the flesh becomes the mother of the eternal fire,
if you understand all this well, desires will immediately flee from you, and a marvelous calm and quiet will come about in your soul,
just as the riot of disorderly and impure maidservants is calmed by the arrival of an honorable and chaste mistress.
Watch over yourself, then, for the one part of your soul is rational and intelligent,
while the other is passionate and irrational; and to the first belongs lordship by nature, and to the others obedience and trust in reason.
Never, then, let your mind be taken captive and enslaved to the passions, nor allow the passions to rise up against reason and take for themselves the lordship of the soul.
But why should I say many things? For if you have well acquired understanding of your own self, it will lead you to the knowledge of God.
For if you watch over yourself, you will have no need of understanding the Creator from other created things,
but within yourself you should see the great wisdom of your Creator.
Understand God incorporeally, as uncircumscribed, by means of that incorporeal soul dwelling within you,
for your mind, too, does not by nature have a fixed abiding in one place, but it is in one place because of its union with the body.
And again, consider your soul, and through it believe that God is invisible, for your soul too is invisible to bodily eyes,
since it has neither color nor form, nor is it seen in any bodily shape, but it is known only from its power and its works.
Therefore do not seek to see God with the eye, but turn your faith inward and hold the vision of him with the mind.

Marvel at the craftsmanship of the Creator: how he united the power of the soul with the body, so that it is spread out to all its extremities and brings those variously divided members together into communion.
Investigate what that power is which is given from the soul to the body, and what that injury is which passes from the body to the soul.
How does the body receive life from the soul, and how in turn does the soul receive injuries from the body?
Or what treasuries of learning does it have, such that the multitude of things to come does not darken the understanding of things past,
but the memories of each matter remain unmixed and separate, and each matter is inscribed in the mind like an image?
And how, when it is entangled in bodily passions, does it swiftly lose its own beauty, or how,
when the stain of wickedness is again washed away by virtues, does it return to the likeness of its own Creator?
If you wish, after the soul, to consider also the constitution of the body, reflect and marvel
at how that good Craftsman created it beautifully as a dwelling for the rational soul,
for of all creatures he created man alone upright, so that he himself might know from his own form that his life comes from that heavenly kinship.
For all quadrupeds look toward the ground and are bent toward the belly, but man is ready to look up to heaven,
so that he may not turn to the concerns of the belly or to its passions, but that all his eagerness may be directed toward the ascent to heaven.
And again, he set the head above everything else, and in it he placed the places of honor of most of the senses, for there are the organs of sight, hearing and smell, and the mouth.
All of them are settled close to one another, and though thus crowded into that small space, none disturbs the work of its neighbor:
for the eyes are settled in the place highest above the other members, so that none of the members of the body should be above them,
yet they are a little below the brows, and so they see everything distinctly;
again, the ears are not opened straight, but the entrance for sounds is turned in many windings.
And this too is a work [?] of the divine wisdom, so that sound may be heard without hindrance, or even more strongly, through that turning within the crookedness of the passage,
while nothing else can fall in from outside and obstruct that sense;
Consider again the nature of the tongue as well, how it is soft and turns easily, and by its many kinds of turning is sufficient for every word;
and again the teeth, which are organs of the voice and firm helpers of the tongue, and also receivers and cutters of food.
And so, if with good reasoning you consider all of this: the entry of the air inward through the organ of breathing,
the settling of heat upon the heart, the organs of digestion, the places and channels of the blood,
from all this you will see the unsearchable wisdom of your Creator, so that you too may say with the prophet: How "your knowledge has become wondrous to me"!
Understand yourself, therefore, so that you may understand God, to whom belongs glory now and always and unto the ages of ages. Amen.
